621.quote_or_event: “Your actions seem so sweet to me.”
621.explanation: In a hymn of Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan says that whatever God does tastes sweet to him. Sikh tradition links this acceptance of God's will (bhana manna) with his calm in the face of torture and martyrdom at Lahore in 1606.
621.tie_back: The Kural tells us to meet trouble with a smile; Guru Arjan meets whatever comes as something sweet, which is the same calm, cheerful acceptance.
621.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 394, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
621._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on meeting hardship with cheerful acceptance; the link to Guru Arjan's martyrdom is a matter of Sikh tradition, not something the verse itself states.

622.quote_or_event: “Remembering God, one is not touched by fear. Remembering God, one does not suffer sorrow.”
622.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan lists the fruits of simran, among them freedom from fear and from sorrow.
622.tie_back: The Kural says a flood of sorrow vanishes once the wise turn a steady mind on it; Guru Arjan says sorrow cannot afflict a mind turned steadily towards God.
622.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 262, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani Sahib), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
622._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on a settled mind overcoming sorrow, but the remedy in Gurbani is remembrance of God (naam simran), not the wise person's own firmness of resolve as in the Kural.

623.quote_or_event: “That man, who in the midst of pain, does not feel pain, who is not affected by pleasure, affection or fear, and who looks alike upon gold and dust;”
623.explanation: In a hymn of Raag Sorath, Guru Tegh Bahadur describes the person who is not shaken by pain even in its midst and who stays the same whatever comes.
623.tie_back: The Kural says those who do not grieve at sorrow turn the tables on sorrow itself; Guru Tegh Bahadur praises the one who, in the midst of pain, does not feel pain.
623.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 633, Raag Sorath, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
623._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on refusing to suffer at suffering; the Kural's playful twist of grief recoiling on grief is absent, and Gurbani roots this steadiness in detachment and the divine Name.

624.quote_or_event: “The mythical bull is Dharma, the son of compassion; this is what patiently holds the earth in its place.”
624.explanation: In Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak takes the old myth of a bull bearing the earth and reinterprets it: the bull is dharma, born of compassion, which patiently bears the world's weight.
624.tie_back: The Kural pictures the steadfast person as an ox hauling the cart through every rut and mire; Japji Sahib turns the bull that patiently carries the load into an image of dharma.
624.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 3, Japji Sahib (pauri 16), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
624._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the shared image is the patient bull bearing a heavy load, but Guru Nanak uses it to explain dharma and cosmic order, not personal endurance of hardship, and he goes on to question the literal myth.

625.quote_or_event: Guru Gobind Singh had to give up Anandpur after a long siege in December 1705, saw his two elder sons die in the battle of Chamkaur, and then learned that his two younger sons had been executed at Sirhind. With only a few companions left, he wrote the Zafarnamah to Emperor Aurangzeb in a mood of unbroken spirit, declaring that the loss of his four children mattered little while the Khalsa still stood.
625.explanation: This run of disasters, coming one after another within a few weeks, is remembered in Sikh history as the supreme test of Guru Gobind Singh's spirit, and his answer was the defiant Zafarnamah rather than despair.
625.tie_back: The Kural says that when troubles come piled one on another, the person who does not break inside makes the troubles themselves suffer; Guru Gobind Singh met a whole cascade of losses without breaking.
625.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (Punjabi University, Patiala, ed. Harbans Singh), 'Zafarnamah', via The Sikh Encyclopedia (paraphrase)
625._accuracy_note: Strong fit on unbroken spirit under successive calamities; the events are well attested, the Zafarnamah is preserved in the Dasam Granth, whose compilation is debated among Sikhs, and the Guru's inner state is described from Sikh tradition.

626.quote_or_event: “If some of this capital is later taken back by the Banker, the ignorant person shows his anger. He himself destroys his own credibility, and he shall not again be trusted.”
626.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan compares all we possess to capital lent by God the Banker; the ignorant person who clings to it as his own grows angry when part of it is taken back.
626.tie_back: The Kural asks whether those who never clung to wealth as their own would wail at its loss; Guru Arjan shows that only the one who treats God's loan as his own rages when it is recalled.
626.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 268, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani Sahib, ashtpadi 5), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
626._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: both trace grief at loss to possessive clinging; Guru Arjan's ground for letting go is that everything belongs to God, a theistic reason the Kural does not give.

627.quote_or_event: “Fareed, I thought that I was in trouble; the whole world is in trouble!”
627.explanation: In a salok of Sheikh Farid included in the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sufi saint realises that suffering is not his alone but the common lot of everyone in the world.
627.tie_back: The Kural says the noble know the body is simply a target for pain and so do not treat it as a calamity; Farid likewise sees pain as the shared lot of all embodied beings.
627.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1382, Salok Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
627._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on suffering as universal to embodied life; Farid speaks of the whole world rather than of the body as a target, and draws the lesson of humility rather than of composure.

628.quote_or_event: “Suffering is the medicine, and pleasure the disease, because where there is pleasure, there is no desire for God.”
628.explanation: In Asa di Vaar, Guru Nanak turns the usual valuation upside down: hardship heals and comfort sickens, because comfort makes a person forget God.
628.tie_back: The Kural praises the one who does not chase pleasure and accepts hardship as natural; Guru Nanak goes further and calls hardship the medicine and pleasure the disease.
628.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 469, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
628._accuracy_note: Strong fit on not craving pleasure and accepting hardship; Guru Nanak's reason is spiritual (pleasure dulls the longing for God), whereas the Kural's is practical freedom from misery.

629.quote_or_event: “One who is not affected by pleasure or pain, who looks upon friend and enemy alike”
629.explanation: In his saloks at the close of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Tegh Bahadur describes the liberated person as one whom neither joy nor sorrow can sway.
629.tie_back: The Kural says one who does not revel in good times will not sink in bad times; Guru Tegh Bahadur praises the one whom neither pleasure nor pain can move.
629.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427, Salok Mahala 9, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
629._accuracy_note: Strong fit on evenness in pleasure and pain; the Kural states it as cause and effect (no revelling, so no sinking), while the salok describes a single settled state, and it adds equal regard for friend and foe.

630.quote_or_event: “If You will bless me with happiness, then I will worship and adore You. Even in pain, I will meditate on You.”
630.explanation: In a hymn of Raag Soohee, Guru Ram Das vows to turn to God in exactly the same way in pain as in happiness.
630.tie_back: The Kural asks us to take hardship as if it were pleasure; Guru Ram Das treats pain and happiness alike as occasions to remember God.
630.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 757, Raag Soohee, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
630._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on treating pain as one treats pleasure; the Kural's promised reward, a distinction admired even by enemies, has no counterpart in this devotional verse.
